clinicalPearls: Numbness of the chin and lower lip in the distribution of the mental (or inferior alveolar) nerve
It is an important red-flag sign because it is frequently caused by underlying malignancy
Recognised causes include metastatic breast and prostate cancer, lymphoma and leukaemic infiltration, and it may herald relapse
Benign causes exist (dental or local trauma, mandibular osteomyelitis, sickle cell disease), but malignancy must be excluded
The lesion may be at the mandible (mental nerve) or more proximally at the skull base or leptomeninges
Investigation targets the whole nerve pathway and a search for systemic malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Numb chin syndrome arises from injury to the mental nerve or its parent inferior alveolar/mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, anywhere from the leptomeninges and skull base to the mandibular canal and mental foramen. Malignant causes act by perineural spread, mandibular or leptomeningeal metastasis, or direct compression, which is why the sign so often reflects cancer. Benign local processes injure the nerve within the mandible. The chin and lip sensory loss reflects the terminal cutaneous territory of the affected nerve.
additionalDifferentials: Dental or mandibular local pathology / trauma
Multiple sclerosis or other trigeminal pathology
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain, skull base and mandible with attention to the trigeminal/mental nerve pathway
Investigation for systemic malignancy (imaging, tumour markers) where a cause is not evident
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis if leptomeningeal disease is suspected
Full blood count and film if leukaemia is considered
redFlags: Known or suspected malignancy (new numb chin may signal metastasis or relapse)
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is driven by the underlying cause; when due to malignancy it often signifies advanced or recurrent disease and a poor outlook, whereas benign causes may resolve.
pitfalls: Dismissing chin numbness as dental without excluding malignancy
Failing to image the entire nerve pathway including the skull base
Overlooking it as a marker of cancer relapse
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Urgent investigation and treatment directed at the underlying cause, most importantly excluding and treating malignancy
Oncological therapy such as chemotherapy, radiotherapy and intrathecal treatment for leptomeningeal disease where metastatic breast, prostate or haematological cancer is identified
Treatment of benign causes such as dental infection, mandibular osteomyelitis or trauma once malignancy is excluded
Neuropathic analgesia for the chin and lip sensory symptoms
Multidisciplinary involvement of oncology, maxillofacial surgery and neurology
Recognition that a new numb chin in a patient with cancer may herald relapse, prompting restaging and escalation
